desc:
Each interval [a, b] is a closed range of integers, containing a, a + 1, ..., b. Choose a set S of integers such that every interval contains at least two elements of S. Return the smallest possible size of S.

intervals = [[1, 4], [2, 3], [6, 9]]  ->  4

For example S = {2, 3, 8, 9}: the first two intervals both contain 2 and 3, and the last contains 8 and 9. Three points are impossible, since [2, 3] and [6, 9] share no integer.
hints: With one point per interval this is the minimum-arrows problem: sort by right end and place a point at the right end of the first unhit interval. What changes if two points are needed?
Sort by right end ascending (ties: left end descending). Remember the last two chosen points and check how many of them lie in the next interval.
If the interval contains neither of the two last points, add its two rightmost integers (b - 1 and b). If it contains only the larger one, add b. If it contains both, do nothing.
editorial: Sort by right end, ties by left end descending, and process in that order, always choosing points as far to the right as possible: for the first interval that is b - 1 and b. A point placed at the right end of the interval being processed is the most useful one, since all later intervals have a right end at least as large and a right-most point has the greatest chance of lying in them (intervals that come later and start at or before the point contain it). This is the arrows argument applied twice.

Keep the two largest chosen points lo < hi. For a new interval [a, b]: if a > hi neither point is inside, so add b - 1 and b (cost 2). Else if a > lo, only hi is inside, so add b (cost 1; the tie-break on the left end guarantees b > hi here). Otherwise both chosen points lie inside and nothing is added. Sorting dominates: O(n log n), O(1) extra space.
